problem_text:
A regional air freight network must schedule a circuit among 7 major terminals:
Terminal Alpha: Positioned at grid reference (88,29)
Terminal Beta: Positioned at grid reference (39,71)
Terminal Gamma: Positioned at grid reference (4,10)
Terminal Delta: Positioned at grid reference (10,52)
Terminal Epsilon: Positioned at grid reference (174,66)
Terminal Zeta: Positioned at grid reference (142,80)
Terminal Eta: Positioned at grid reference (93,145)

The flight distances between terminals, measured in nautical miles, are predetermined:
Alpha to Gamma: 86.1 nm
Alpha to Delta: 81.3 nm
Alpha to Epsilon: 93.6 nm
Alpha to Zeta: 74.3 nm
Alpha to Eta: 116.1 nm
Beta to Gamma: 70.3 nm
Beta to Delta: 34.7 nm
Beta to Epsilon: 135.1 nm
Beta to Zeta: 103.4 nm
Beta to Eta: 91.6 nm
Gamma to Delta: 42.4 nm
Gamma to Epsilon: 179.0 nm
Gamma to Zeta: 154.7 nm
Gamma to Eta: 161.7 nm
Delta to Epsilon: 164.6 nm
Delta to Zeta: 134.9 nm
Delta to Eta: 124.7 nm
Epsilon to Zeta: 34.9 nm
Epsilon to Eta: 113.1 nm
Zeta to Eta: 81.4 nm

Due to airspace restrictions, a direct flight corridor between Terminal Alpha and Terminal Beta is unavailable.
Furthermore, operational regulations mandate that exactly one of the following two flight segments must be incorporated into the circuit: the segment between Terminal Beta and Terminal Gamma, or the segment between Terminal Gamma and Terminal Delta.

The objective is to determine the most fuel-efficient closed routing, where each terminal is serviced precisely once before returning to the origin.
